nameStory: Blue mistflower gets its name from its soft, misty-blue flowers that bloom in late summer like a gentle cloud of color. The 'mist' part refers to the fuzzy, delicate appearance of its clustered blooms, while 'flower' is obvious! It's also called wild ageratum because its flowers look remarkably similar to the popular garden annual ageratum.
description: Blue mistflower is a native wildflower that forms spreading patches of soft blue blooms in late summer and fall. This herbaceous perennial grows 1-3 feet tall with heart-shaped, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs along sturdy stems. The plant produces clusters of fuzzy, powder-blue flowers that lack the typical daisy petals you might expect from the sunflower family. Instead, each 'flower' is actually a tight bundle of tiny tubular florets that give the whole cluster a soft, cotton-candy appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Fluffy clusters of powder-blue to violet-blue flowers with no petals - just fuzzy tubular florets that feel soft to touch and create a misty appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Heart-shaped to triangular leaves with toothed edges, arranged in opposite pairs, feeling slightly rough and wrinkled like fine sandpaper

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies through underground rhizomes, creating patches of plants 1-3 feet tall with multiple branching stems

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny seeds topped with white, fluffy bristles (like dandelion parachutes) that catch the wind and drift away in fall

habitat: Blue mistflower thrives in moist to wet soils along stream banks, pond edges, wet meadows, and roadside ditches throughout New England. It prefers partial shade to full sun and is often found growing alongside other moisture-loving plants like jewelweed, cardinal flower, and various sedges. You'll spot it most commonly in low-lying areas that stay consistently moist.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground rhizomes as triangular, wrinkled leaves on reddish stems. Plants form low, spreading mounds of foliage.
seasonality.summer: Leaves reach full size and plants grow taller, but the real show begins in late summer when flower buds start forming at stem tips.
seasonality.fall: Peak bloom time! Clusters of misty blue flowers create stunning displays from August through October, followed by fluffy white seed heads that persist into late fall.
seasonality.winter: Plants die back completely to underground rhizomes, leaving no above-ground trace except for dried stems in protected areas.

funFact: Blue mistflower is like a butterfly magnet with a sweet tooth - its flowers contain so much nectar that monarchs, skippers, and other butterflies will actually fight over the best patches during their fall migration!
confusionNotes: Blue mistflower is most often confused with garden ageratum, but wild mistflower has heart-shaped, toothed leaves (ageratum's are more oval and smooth-edged) and grows much taller. Remember: 'Wild and tall with toothed leaves' versus 'tame and small with smooth leaves.'
contextualKnowledge: This plant was shuffled around botanically and used to be classified in the genus Eupatorium (the bonesets), which is why you might see it called 'blue boneset' in older field guides. Modern DNA studies showed it deserved its own genus, Conoclinium, making it quite special as the only member of this genus in our region.
compareHints: Blue mistflower is the only species in its genus Conoclinium found in New England, making it unique among our native wildflowers. Its closest relatives are the white-flowered bonesets (Eupatorium species), but those have white flowers and typically more lance-shaped leaves. Among blue-flowered plants in the aster family, mistflower stands out because it completely lacks the petal-like ray flowers that most of its relatives display.
